name: English (West Midlands)
variety: Urban English of the West Midlands conurbation: Birmingham ('Brummie') with the neighbouring Black Country
sources: Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Volume 2: The British Isles. Cambridge University Press.
Clark, Urszula (2004). The English West Midlands: phonology. In Schneider et al. (eds.), A Handbook of Varieties of English, volume 1. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.

Mathisen, Anne Grethe (1999). Sandwell, West Midlands: ambiguous perspectives on gender patterns and models of change. In Foulkes and Docherty (eds.), Urban Voices: Accent Studies in the British Isles. London: Arnold.
Thorne, Steve (2003). Birmingham English: A Sociolinguistic Study. Doctoral dissertation, University of Birmingham.
Hughes, Arthur; Trudgill, Peter; Watt, Dominic (2012). English Accents and Dialects. 5th edition. London: Hodder Education.
Cruttenden, Alan (1997). Intonation. 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.
contrasts: no FOOT-STRUT split: STRUT words have a vowel at or near that of FOOT, [ʊ] or an unrounded [ɤ] (put = putt)
no TRAP-BATH split: BATH words have the short vowel of TRAP, [a]
non-rhotic, with long vowels and centring diphthongs where the spelling has r
wide diphthongs in FLEECE, GOOSE, FACE, GOAT, PRICE and MOUTH, shifted in the same direction as in London
PRICE [ɔi] is close to CHOICE [oi] and merges with it for some speakers
lexical stress with reduction of unstressed vowels
allophony: KIT is very close, near [i], and FLEECE is a diphthong [əi] or [ɪi]
GOOSE is a diphthong with a central start, [əʉ]
FACE is [æi] or [ʌi], GOAT is [ʌʊ], PRICE is [ɔi] or [ɒi], MOUTH is [æʊ] or [ɛʊ]
final unstressed happY is a diphthong [əi] or a long [iː]
ng is [ŋɡ], also at the end of a word and before a suffix (sing [sɪŋɡ], singer [ˈsɪŋɡə], singing)
/ɹ/ is a postalveolar approximant; older speakers may use a tap between vowels; linking and intrusive /r/ are used
/t/ before a consonant or pause is often a glottal stop, and /t/ between vowels across a word boundary may be [ɹ]
/l/ is clear before vowels and dark after them
NURSE is [ɜː], close and fronted for some speakers; SQUARE is a long monophthong [ɛː]
in the Black Country some words with a before a nasal have [ɒ] (man, hand) and the verb forms differ from the standard; these are dialect features outside the urban accent described here
phonotactics: [ŋ] is always followed by [ɡ] or [k], so it is the form of /n/ before a velar stop and not a separate phoneme
short vowels need a following consonant in a stressed syllable
/h/, where kept, only begins a syllable

stress.rule: As in other accents of English: fixed for each word, with Germanic initial stress and weight-sensitive Latinate stress.
stress.cues: pitch movement on accented syllables, duration, loudness and vowel quality

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong, with schwa and [ɪ] in unstressed syllables
rhythm.notes: I know of no nPVI value for this accent.

length.notes: Long monophthongs /ɑː ɔː ɜː ɛː/ contrast with short vowels; the other long vowels of RP are diphthongs here. No long consonants.

intonation.declarative: statements often have a low accented syllable followed by a rise that is held as a high plateau, with or without a slight fall at the very end; plain falls also occur
intonation.yes_no_question: rise, with a contour close to that of statements
intonation.wh_question: fall, or the rise plus plateau of statements
intonation.accent_shape: L* H: low on the accented syllable, rise on the following syllables, then level
intonation.notes: Birmingham is one of the cities with rising statement tunes ('urban north British' rises) in Cruttenden (1997), beside Belfast, Glasgow, Liverpool and Tyneside. The accent is often heard as flat, with small pitch movements and a downward drift.

phonation: glottal replacement of /t/ before consonants and pause

problems: [ŋɡ] is produced only before a vowel (singing is [sɪŋɡɪŋ]); at the end of a word the accent also has [ŋɡ]
SQUARE is the central vowel [ɜː] (formant file vowel/3_en) and NURSE a front rounded vowel (vowel/y#); the descriptions have [ɛː] for SQUARE and [ɜː] for NURSE
FACE is labelled [eː] in the IPA trace although its formant data are those of a wide diphthong (vdiph/@i_3)
STRUT and FOOT are both labelled [ʊ] but use different formant files
/h/ is removed everywhere ('replace 00 h NULL'); in speech h-dropping is variable and depends on style
KIT has the usual lax quality, not the very close vowel of Birmingham
the rising tune (intonation group 4) is applied to every statement and the same final movement to every clause; there is no rise plus plateau and no choice between rising and falling statements
there is no glottal replacement of /t/
good: the shifted diphthongs are present: FLEECE [ei]-like, GOOSE [əu], PRICE [ɔɪ], CHOICE [oɪ], GOAT [ʌʊ], MOUTH [æʊ]
STRUT has the FOOT vowel and BATH the short [a]
statements end in a rise, which matches the rising statement tunes reported for Birmingham
final unstressed happY is a long close vowel

notes: The vowel qualities follow Wells (1982) and Clark (2004); both stress that Birmingham and the Black Country differ in detail and that speakers vary with class and age. I give no formant, voice onset time or duration values because I know of no published measurements for this accent that I can quote.
